B5-U6-Q038.text: Incremental backups backup all data that has changed since the previous backup. Incremental backups do clear the archive bit. These backups are relatively fast because there is less data being backed up each time as compared to full and differential backups. B5-X-U6-Q005.text:
Full Backup

This backup type backs up all files and folders. It does not rely on the archive bit to tell it what to backup, but it does clear the bit as each file is backed up

B5-X-U6-Q006.text: Differential backups back up everything that has changed since the most recent full backup. Differential backups do not clear the archive bit. Differential backs take longer to perform because more data is backed up every time the differential backup takes place

B5-X-U6-Q007.text: Incremental backups do take more time to restore because the full backup must be restored first followed by every incremental backup in the order they were made

Incremental backups backup all data that has changed since the previous backup. Incremental backups do clear the archive bit. These backups are relatively fast because there is less data being backed up each time as compared to full and differential backups

B5-X-U7-Q004.text:
Setting file permissions on data is not sufficient alone to maintain confidentiality, because most organizations store information on a server, and users access the data from their client computers across the network. Permissions ensure that only the appropriate user accounts can get access to files.

However, when users download those files to their computers across the network, file permissions do not protect the file contents from being read while the files are in transit. This is where encryption comes in—encrypting data puts the information in an unreadable format until an authorized person decrypts the data, which places it back in a readable format

B5-X-U7-Q006.text: Data integrity also means that if you store a file on a storage drive and open it later, you can be certain that the data has not been altered while in storage

B5-X-U7-Q007.text: To ensure data integrity when communicating over a network, the sending system runs the data through a mathematical algorithm, known as a hashing algorithm, which then generates an answer, known as the hash value
Once the destination system has its own calculated hash value, it then compares that to the hash value sent with the message—if they are the same, then it is assumed the data has not been altered
